candidate_findings.message: On Android, a non-seekable Stream (for example a network or pipe stream passed straight to MediaSource.FromStream) never plays: Open treats ExoPlayer's 'length unknown' value as an error and throws. The other platforms also reject such streams, and the public API neither checks for this nor documents it. The StreamDataSource constructor sets `length = stream.CanSeek ? stream.Length : C.LengthUnset`. Open computes `bytesRemaining = dataSpec.Length != C.LengthUnset ? dataSpec.Length : (length != C.LengthUnset ? length - dataSpec.Position : C.LengthUnset)`. A progressive load at position 0 has no DataSpec length, so for a non-seekable stream this gives C.LengthUnset (-1). The next line, `if (bytesRemaining < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(... "Position {dataSpec.Position} exceeds stream length {length}.")`, then fires. Read() has `bytesRemaining != C.LengthUnset` branches, which shows unknown length was meant to be supported. On Windows, `streamMediaSource.Stream.AsRandomAccessStream()` (MediaManager.windows.cs:343) needs a seekable stream. On Apple, FillContentInformation sets `ContentLength = stream.CanSeek ? stream.Length : 0`. `MediaSource.FromStream(Stream stream)` has no CanSeek check, and its XML doc doesn't mention seekability.

On iOS/macOS, when reading the stream fails (for example the app has disposed it, or an IO error), the resource loader swallows the exception and still reports the request as finished successfully. AVFoundation gets no error, MediaFailed carries no cause, and in Release builds nothing is logged at all. FillDataRequest wraps the seek and read in `catch (Exception ex) { System.Diagnostics.Debug.WriteLine($"Error reading stream data: {ex.Message}"); }`. Debug.WriteLine is [Conditional("DEBUG")], so a Release-built package drops the call. ShouldWaitForLoadingOfRequestedResource then always calls `loadingRequest.FinishLoading();` (line 35) and never `FinishLoadingWithError`. The class has no access to the MediaManager Logger.

The Apple loader allocates a managed buffer the size of each AVFoundation data request and copies it twice. A request for the rest of a large video can therefore allocate hundreds of MB, and for resources over 2 GB the int cast overflows and the load fails silently. If a single Read returns less than was asked, the request is still marked complete with the rest missing. `var requestedLength = (int)dataRequest.RequestedLength;` then `var buffer = new byte[requestedLength]; var bytesRead = stream.Read(buffer, 0, requestedLength);` then `NSData.FromArray(buffer[..bytesRead])`. The range slice copies once and NSData.FromArray copies again. There is one `dataRequest.Respond(data)` with no chunked loop, followed by `loadingRequest.FinishLoading()`. The OverflowException from a negative size is caught by the swallowing catch.

On iOS/macOS every stream except a QuickTime ftyp is declared to AVFoundation as "public.mpeg-4", so audio streams such as MP3, WAV or FLAC may fail to open. The change adds and tests a fuller magic-number sniffer but uses it only on Windows. GetStreamContentType returns "com.apple.quicktime-movie" only when the ftyp brand starts with "qt". Every other path returns `StreamAssetResourceLoader.DefaultContentType` or the hard-coded `"public.mpeg-4"`, and FillContentInformation passes that value to `contentInformationRequest.ContentType`. StreamExtensions.GetMimeType (shared file, covered by StreamExtensionsTests) already detects ID3/MPEG audio, RIFF WAVE, FLAC, Ogg and WebM, but its only caller is MediaManager.windows.cs:344.

On Android, setting a StreamMediaSource's Stream to null replays the previous stream instead of clearing playback. If the app has already disposed that stream, the player then reads a disposed object. StreamMediaSource's StreamProperty propertyChanged calls OnSourceChanged, which MediaElement forwards as a Source property change. PlatformUpdateSource disposes currentStreamDataSourceFactory only when `MediaElement.Source is not StreamMediaSource` (line 379). In SetPlayerData, `case StreamMediaSource` breaks when `Stream is null` and falls through to `return mediaItem;` (line 765), and that field still holds the previous stream's builder. Line 395, `if (currentStreamDataSourceFactory is not null && MediaElement.Source is StreamMediaSource)`, then wraps the old factory in a new ProgressiveMediaSource, calls Prepare and raises MediaOpened. On iOS the same input sets PlayerItem to null.

When an Android player switches from a stream to another source type, the StreamDataSourceFactory Java peer is disposed while the old ProgressiveMediaSource still references it. If ExoPlayer creates a period from it during the await that follows, the app may crash. Lines 379-383 call `currentStreamDataSourceFactory?.Dispose()` before `await SetPlayerData(...)` (line 389). SetPlayerData awaits GetBytesFromMetadataArtworkUrl, which makes HTTP HEAD and GET requests when artwork is set. Only after that does Player.SetMediaItem or SetMediaSource (lines 409/413) replace the old source built with `new ProgressiveMediaSource.Factory(currentStreamDataSourceFactory)`. StreamDataSourceFactory has no (IntPtr, JniHandleOwnership) constructor for re-activation.

The new sample page crashes the app if it is opened offline or the download fails, because the network call in the async void OnAppearing has no try/catch. The Open Video and Record Video handlers have the same problem with picker or permission failures, and with capture on devices or simulators that have no camera. `protected override async void OnAppearing() { base.OnAppearing(); await using var networkStream = await httpClient.GetStreamAsync(StreamingUrls.BuckBunny); await UpdateSourceStream(networkStream); }`: only UpdateSourceStream catches exceptions. OnOpenVideoClicked (`await MediaPicker.Default.PickVideosAsync(pickerOptions)`) and OnRecordVideoClicked (`await MediaPicker.Default.CaptureVideoAsync(...)`, with no IsCaptureSupported check) are async void with no exception handling.

The sample's stream swap isn't serialised. If the initial download is still running when the user picks or records a video, the two UpdateSourceStream calls can dispose each other's stream, rewind or play the wrong stream, or replace the user's video with the downloaded one. The stream that is currently playing is also disposed before its replacement is ready. sourceStreamSemaphore is held only inside ReleaseSourceStream, around the dispose. UpdateSourceStream assigns `sourceStream = new MemoryStream()`, awaits `stream.CopyToAsync(sourceStream)`, then reads the field again for `sourceStream.Position = 0` and `MediaSource.FromStream(sourceStream)`. If a second call runs in between, the first call acts on the second call's stream. ReleaseSourceStream (line 173) disposes the MemoryStream that is still MediaElement.Source before the 30 MB replacement download finishes. OnDisappearing (line 51) also disposes it without stopping the player.

The page is registered as transient and implements IAsyncDisposable, so the DI container tracks every instance until its scope ends. Each visit may keep a page and its MediaElement alive, and DisposeAsync never runs when the user navigates away. `public sealed partial class MediaElementFromStreamPage : BasePage<MediaElementFromStreamViewModel>, IAsyncDisposable` is registered with `services.AddTransientWithShellRoute<MediaElementFromStreamPage, MediaElementFromStreamViewModel>()`, which calls `.AddTransient<TView>()` (ServiceCollectionExtensions.shared.cs:136-138). Microsoft DI keeps disposable transients alive until the scope is disposed. No other sample page implements IDisposable or IAsyncDisposable. `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)` in a sealed class with no finalizer does nothing.

The typed HttpClient and retry handler registered for MediaElementFromStreamPage are overridden by the later transient page registration, so the page receives the default HttpClient without the resilience handler. `builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MediaElementFromStreamPage>().AddStandardResilienceHandler(...)` runs before RegisterViewsAndViewModels. That later calls `AddTransientWithShellRoute<MediaElementFromStreamPage, ...>`, which ends in `services.AddTransient<TView>()`. The last registration wins and builds the page with the plain HttpClient that AddHttpClient registers for the default client.

The change edits a locked baseline acceptance test that has nothing to do with the story. The edit is a timing fix and doesn't weaken the assertion, but a judging test was changed inside the change it judges. The diff replaces `await Task.Delay(100, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken);` with `while (!cts.Token.IsCancellationRequested) { await Task.Delay(1, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); }` in LoadViewAsync_CancellationTokenExpired. acceptance.md: "The baseline's tests are the locked acceptance tests". The baseline file MediaSourceTests.cs is also modified (a test is added).

StreamMediaSource's behaviour is covered only by a type check. Source-change propagation, the implicit conversions, the converter output and the Android data-source logic (where the non-seekable bug is) have no tests. The only MediaElement test added is MediaSourceFromStreamShouldBeStreamMediaSource, which asserts `mediaSource.Should().BeAssignableTo<StreamMediaSource>()`. No test sets StreamMediaSource.Stream and checks for a source-change notification. Nothing exercises `implicit operator StreamMediaSource?(Stream?)`, ToString, or the new `StreamMediaSource => ToString()` arm of MediaSourceConverter.ConvertTo. StreamDataSource.Open and Read are untested. StreamExtensionsTests covers only the sniffer that Windows uses.

The MIME sniffer labels any stream whose first byte is 0x47 as MPEG-TS and treats ADTS AAC headers as MP3, and a test locks in the ADTS case. Windows may therefore pass the wrong content type to the media pipeline. `if (header.Length >= 1 && header[0] is 0x47) return "video/mp2t";` checks a single byte, although the TS sync byte repeats every 188 bytes. `if (header.Length >= 2 && header[0] is 0xFF && (header[1] & 0xE0) is 0xE0) return "audio/mpeg";` also matches ADTS AAC (layer bits 00, e.g. 0xFFF0/0xFFF1). StreamExtensionsTests has `[InlineData(0xF0)]` expecting "audio/mpeg".

FromStream is inconsistent with the other factory methods, and nothing documents the stream's ownership or requirements, so callers can't tell that they must keep the stream open and seekable, must dispose it themselves, or that Tizen throws. `public static StreamMediaSource FromStream(Stream stream) => new StreamMediaSource { Stream = stream };` returns StreamMediaSource, whereas FromFile, FromUri and FromResource return MediaSource. It has no ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull, although FromUri does and this diff adds a codestyle rule preferring it. Neither the XML docs of FromStream nor those of StreamMediaSource mention seekability, lifetime (the platform classes only have code comments: "let the caller manage its lifetime") or the Tizen `throw new NotSupportedException`. StreamExtensions' summary says "on Windows platform", but it lives in a .shared.cs file.

The change edits the coding agent's instruction file without the story asking for it, adding a new style rule that future agent runs will follow. The diff adds a "## Argument Validation:" section that prefers `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` over manual null checks, and deletes the file's trailing ``` line. The content is harmless (the fence count is now balanced), but it is an unreviewed instruction-file change.

Untested behaviour changes unrelated to stream support ride along with the feature: Android's HttpClient lifetime and the artwork file-open mode change, alongside pure reorders and reformatting. `static readonly HttpClient client = new();` becomes `readonly HttpClient client = new();`, so each MediaManager gets its own HttpClient (the baseline disposed the shared static client in instance Dispose). `File.Open(normalizedFilePath, FileMode.Create)` becomes `File.OpenRead(normalizedFilePath)` at line 617; the baseline truncated local artwork files, so this is a real fix, but it has no test. Implicit operators are moved in FileMediaSource, ResourceMediaSource and UriMediaSource. Each PlayerListener stub is expanded from one line to three. PopupsPage.xaml.cs has a whitespace-only change.

The new sample page copies MediaElementPage's controls and handlers, reuses the title "MediaElement", and its unlabelled "-"/"+" buttons give screen-reader users no context. MediaElementFromStreamPage.xaml.cs repeats OnSpeedMinusClicked, OnSpeedPlusClicked, OnVolumeMinusClicked, OnVolumePlusClicked, the slider drag handlers and MediaElement_PropertyChanged verbatim from MediaElementPage.xaml.cs. The XAML has `Title="MediaElement"`. `<Button Text="-" Clicked="OnSpeedMinusClicked" />`, `<Button Text="+" .../>` and the volume pair have no SemanticProperties.Description.

Git-install detection now treats any directory with a `.git` four levels above the CLI module as an Agent Orchestrator checkout. A CLI copy sitting outside node_modules inside some other git repo is therefore classified "git", and `ao update` then runs the update script against that unrelated repo. The diff removes the `existsSync(resolve(repoRoot, "scripts/ao-update.sh"))` marker and keeps only `if (existsSync(resolve(repoRoot, ".git")))`. Nothing replaces the marker, although the script still exists at `packages/cli/src/assets/scripts/ao-update.sh` and could have been checked there. Trigger: the CLI package copied (vendored) into another monorepo, e.g. `other-repo/packages/cli/dist/lib/update-check.js`. `classifyInstallPath` returns "git". In `handleGitUpdate`, `hasRepoScript("ao-update.sh")` is still true because the bundled copy sits in `dist/assets/scripts`, so the npm fallback never fires. `runRepoScript` passes `AO_REPO_ROOT` = `resolveDefaultRepoRootFromPath` = `../../../../` = `other-repo`. `ao-update.sh` then runs `cd "$REPO_ROOT"`, `git pull --ff-only origin main`, `pnpm install` and `pnpm --filter @aoagents/ao-cli clean/build` in that repo. The diff also deletes the update-check tests "returns 'unknown' when .git exists but scripts/ao-update.sh does not" and "…when scripts/ao-update.sh exists but .git does not", so nothing guards this any more.

After the move, both scripts' fallback for locating themselves now points at the `assets/` directory instead of the repo or package root. Running either script directly, without the CLI, uses the wrong root. Because the CLI always sets the root, the doctor script's new layout auto-detection is never reached when the CLI runs it. `REPO_ROOT="${AO_REPO_ROOT:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)}"` (also `ao-doctor.sh:31`) was correct when the file lived at `scripts/`. Now it resolves to `packages/cli/src/assets` or `<pkg>/dist/assets`. If `ao-update.sh` is run directly, `cd "$REPO_ROOT"` lands inside the work tree, so `git rev-parse` passes. `git pull` and `pnpm install` then run before `cd "$REPO_ROOT/packages/ao"` fails partway through. `ao-doctor.sh:33-39` detects the package-install layout from `$REPO_ROOT/package.json`/`dist/index.js`, which the stale default can never satisfy. `runRepoScript` always exports `AO_REPO_ROOT` and `AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT`, so that branch is dead code under the CLI.

When the update script is missing, the fallback passes a git-install user into the npm flow. That user is told their git-only flags "only apply to git source installs", and gets an npm-version "already latest" verdict that says nothing about whether their checkout is behind main. `handleGitUpdate` calls `handleNpmUpdate(opts, "npm-global")` with the original `opts`. `handleNpmUpdate` then prints `"--skip-smoke and --smoke-only only apply to git source installs. Ignoring."` to a user whose install was just detected as "git". It also returns `Already on latest version` whenever `info.isOutdated` is false, and that flag only compares `package.json` versions with the registry.

The packaged-install doctor test only tries the easy input combination. It never checks that pnpm is downgraded to optional, or that the script detects its own layout, so a regression that again fails npm users who lack pnpm would still pass. The test sets `AO_SCRIPT_LAYOUT: "package-install"` explicitly, which skips the heuristic at `ao-doctor.sh:33-39`. It also calls `createHealthyPath(binDir)`, which installs a fake `pnpm`, so `check_pnpm` passes whether `pnpm_requirement` is "required" or "optional". No test runs the packaged layout without pnpm on PATH.

The regex-escaping helper in the missing-script test escapes nothing. The test therefore relies on path characters happening to match themselves, and it will fail or throw on a checkout path containing characters such as `(`, `+` or `[`. In `expectedScriptsDir.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\\]\\\\]/g, "\\$&")` the character class closes at the first `]` after `\\`. The pattern therefore matches one special character followed by a literal `\\]`, which never occurs in a path, so `replace` returns the path unchanged before it is put into `new RegExp(...)`.

Several names in the script runner no longer describe what they hold, which invites misuse. `hasRepoScript` checks `CLI_DIST_ROOT/assets/scripts`, a file bundled in the CLI package, not anything in a repo. `resolveRepoRoot()` and the exported `AO_REPO_ROOT` now return the npm package directory for package installs. `CLI_DIST_ROOT` is `packages/cli/src` when the CLI runs from source via tsx.

When the CLI runs `ao doctor`, its "bundled doctor script is available" check can never fail, because it tests for the very file that is running. `runRepoScript` resolves the script as `resolve(CLI_DIST_ROOT, "assets", "scripts", "ao-doctor.sh")` = `<pkg>/dist/assets/scripts/ao-doctor.sh`, and passes `AO_REPO_ROOT=<pkg>`. The check `[ -f "$REPO_ROOT/dist/assets/scripts/ao-doctor.sh" ]` therefore tests the script that is currently executing.

Rotation rendering was added only to the deprecated ShapeLayer, which the app never registers, so the renderers the app actually uses still draw shapes unrotated while every wrapped hit test now un-rotates the pointer; on a rotated shape, clicking the visible shape misses it and clicking empty canvas selects it. canvas-engine/src/index.ts:4 marks ShapeLayer `@deprecated Use createDomRendererPlugin`, and apps/web/src/app.tsx:64-65 registers `createGpuRendererPlugin()` and `createDomRendererPlugin()`. dom-renderer/src/dom-shape-layer.tsx:25-34 sets no `transform`, and gpu-renderer/src/shaders/rect.wgsl fs_main reads only params.x/y/z, so the rotation that rectGpuPrimitive packs into params.w is ignored. Meanwhile shape-basic plugin.tsx:46-53 wraps every hit test in withRotation. Trace: a 200x40 rectangle at (0,0) with rotation 90 (set through the debug HUD `rot` field in shapes-panel.tsx:223-229, or arriving in synced data) is drawn horizontally. A click at (190,20) is un-rotated about (100,20) to (100,-70), so aabbHitTest returns false. A click at (100,-70), which is empty canvas as drawn, maps to (10,20) and returns true. gpu-shape-layer.tsx:76-80 hover also stays on the unrotated AABB.

Rotation support is only partly wired: marquee selection, the selection overlay and handles, resize, export, thumbnails and several shape types still treat rotated shapes as unrotated, so they disagree with the new rotated hit tests and the rotated spatial-index bounds. findShapesInRect (tool-select plugin.tsx:98-101) uses `def.getBounds(data)`, which for text and the other plugins returns plain x/y/width/height (text plugin.tsx:109-111). selection-overlay.tsx:39-50 draws an unrotated rect from getShapeBounds. resize-utils.ts never calls deltaToLocal. plugins/usketch-plugin-export/src/exporter.ts:62 emits only `translate(${shape.x}, ${shape.y})`. apps/server/src/rooms/thumbnail-handler.ts:33-46 drops `rotation`. The hit tests for freedraw, frame, connector, counter, island, group and board-portal are not wrapped in withRotation (they register `hitTest` directly). Only board-store.ts:34-39 shapeToBounds uses getRotatedAABB.

The new rejection of corrupt client updates only works when a Y.Doc already exists; in a normal session no doc exists yet, so applyClientUpdate returns true and malformed updates are still buffered, broadcast, tracked and persisted, where they can push real history out of the 500-entry buffer. applyClientUpdate runs `Y.applyUpdate` only inside `if (doc) { ... }` and otherwise falls through to `return true;`. `doc` is set only by getOrCreateDoc, which only the AI handlers, /thumbnail and snapshots call. BoardRoom.fetch (board-room.ts:36-37) calls only loadUpdates/loadFromStorage. So in webSocketMessage (board-room.ts:118-126), `applied` is true and pushUpdate, trackUpdate, broadcast and scheduleSave all run on a corrupt payload. pushUpdate trims to `updates.slice(-MAX_UPDATES_BUFFER)`.

The withRotation tests cannot tell a working wrapper from a no-op: `withRotation = (fn) => fn` passes all four, so nothing in the suite checks that hit tests actually account for rotation. The 'rotation=90' case rotates a 100x100 square by 90°, which maps the square onto itself, and its probe points (50,50) inside and (150,50) outside give the same answer whether or not the point is un-rotated. The 'NaN rotation' case (line 213) uses `alwaysTrue`, which returns true whatever point it receives. No case uses a non-square shape or a non-symmetric angle, which is the only kind of input that would catch a wrong or missing un-rotation (or a reversed sign).

The change may not deliver user-facing rotation: no tool or handle sets `rotation`, and the helpers a rotate/resize interaction would need (deltaToLocal, snapAngle, normalizeAngle) are exported but never called outside the tests. A grep for deltaToLocal|snapAngle|normalizeAngle across packages/plugins/apps src finds them only in rotation.ts, index.ts and rotation.test.ts. The deltaToLocal doc comment says `回転中のリサイズで使用` (used for resize while rotated), but resize-utils.ts and the plugins' `resize` functions never call it. plugins/usketch-plugin-tool-select contains no rotation code. In production nothing writes a non-zero rotation (the debug HUD is DEV-only per app.tsx:70 and shows the field only `shape.rotation !== undefined`). Whether this misses an acceptance criterion can't be checked because story.md isn't available.

Double-click-to-edit detection for text and sticky shapes still calls the unwrapped hit test, so on a rotated shape the area that selects it and the area that enters edit mode differ. Registration uses `hitTest: withRotation(hitTest)` (text plugin.tsx:270, sticky plugin.tsx:478), but the canvas:pointerdown listeners call the raw `hitTest(shape, event.worldPoint)` (text plugin.tsx:249, sticky plugin.tsx:448).

Moving the debounce-flag reset into `finally` after the awaited put means an update that arrives while the put is in flight doesn't schedule another save, and a failed put is only logged and not retried, so the latest edits may stay unpersisted until some later edit happens. The old code set `saveScheduled = false` when the timer fired, before taking the snapshot. Now `saveScheduled = false` runs in `finally` after `await deps.storage.put(...)`, and `scheduleSave` returns early while it is true. The catch only does `console.error("[BoardRoom] Failed to persist Yjs updates:", e)` and schedules no retry. partition-manager.ts:46-59 does the same with `saveScheduled.set(partitionName, false)`. Durable Object input gates may close the in-flight window. The no-retry path remains.

trackUpdate now writes partition_meta whenever in-memory meta is null, but the WebSocket message path never loads stored meta first; if the object's memory is reset while hibernatable sockets stay attached, the first update may overwrite stored meta with only the current quarter and orphan older partitions. trackUpdate sets `metaChanged = true` when `!partitionMeta` and calls `void savePartitionMeta()`, which puts `partition_meta`. webSocketMessage (board-room.ts:107-126) never calls `partitions.loadFromStorage()`; only fetch (board-room.ts:37) does. Sockets are accepted with `this.ctx.acceptWebSocket` (board-room.ts:89), the hibernation API. Before this change, trackUpdate did not save meta, so stored meta survived that path.

The new angle helpers return wrong values on simple edge inputs: normalizeAngle(-360) returns -0, and snapAngle with step 0 returns NaN. `const mod = deg % 360; return mod < 0 ? mod + 360 : mod;`: -360 % 360 is -0, and `-0 < 0` is false, so -0 is returned (Object.is(-0, 0) is false, so a `toBe(0)` check would fail). snapAngle computes `Math.round(deg / step) * step` without guarding step, so step 0 gives NaN. Neither case is tested.

Only the pure rotation helpers are tested; the changed persistence, update-rejection, store-bounds, renderer and plugin wiring ship with no tests. The only test file in the diff is packages/shared/src/__tests__/rotation.test.ts. A glob for apps/server/src/**/*.test.ts finds nothing, so the yjs-sync loadPromise/scheduleSave changes, the partition-manager debounce and meta save, the board-room `applied` gate and the thumbnail-handler type checks are untested. No test covers board-store shapeToBounds with rotation or the withRotation wrapping in the plugins.

The change makes `rotation` mean degrees but leaves the field without a stated unit, while existing docs say radians, and the new public rotation API is undocumented. shape-layer.tsx uses `rotate(${rotation}deg)` and withRotation uses `(rotation * Math.PI) / 180`, but `rotation?: number;` in shape.ts and apps/docs reference/shared.mdx:48 states no unit, and docs/v1/api/README.md:86 says `rotation: number;  // ラジアン` (radians). The new exports in packages/shared/src/index.ts (withRotation, getRotatedAABB, safeRotation, ...) are not mentioned in apps/docs.

The new early return in SMP vTaskSwitchContext also refuses voluntary context switches. A task with preemption disabled that calls vTaskDelay, blocks on a queue or semaphore, calls vTaskSuspend(NULL) or calls vTaskDelete(NULL) keeps running, although the kernel has already moved it to the delayed, suspended or termination list. The new branch `if( pxCurrentTCBs[ xCoreID ]->xPreemptionDisable != pdFALSE ) { xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ] = pdTRUE; } else` is taken before taskSELECT_HIGHEST_PRIORITY_TASK (line 5293), and it cannot tell preemption apart from a voluntary block. Trigger: a task calls vTaskPreemptionDisable(NULL) and then vTaskDelay(10). vTaskDelay calls prvAddCurrentTaskToDelayedList (line 2491), which takes the task off the ready list. It then calls taskYIELD_WITHIN_API (line 2504), which goes through vTaskYieldWithinAPI and portYIELD (line 7004) into vTaskSwitchContext. The switch is now refused and vTaskDelay returns at once. vTaskDelete(NULL) has the same problem: it puts the task on xTasksWaitingTermination (line 2281) and yields (line 2320). The yield is refused, so vTaskDelete returns into the task it just deleted. A blocking queue call with portMAX_DELAY loops back and calls vTaskPlaceOnEventList again while the task's event list item is still on the event list, which may corrupt that list. In the baseline, vTaskSwitchContext had no such check, so these calls blocked correctly. task.h (lines 1425-1453) documents preemption-disable only as protection from being preempted.

When another core suspends or deletes a task that is running with preemption disabled (or changes its core affinity, or ends a priority inheritance), the task stays in the taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD run state permanently. Its next taskENTER_CRITICAL or vTaskSuspendAll then spins forever in prvCheckForRunStateChange, which hangs that core and lets a suspended or deleted task keep running. prvYieldCore (lines 360-364) sets `xTaskRunState = taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD` and sends a single portYIELD_CORE. The callers that do this for a task on another core are vTaskSuspend (line 3239), vTaskDelete (line 2324), vTaskCoreAffinitySet (line 3046) and the priority-disinherit paths (lines 6828 and 6955). On the target core, the new branch in vTaskSwitchContext returns before prvSelectHighestPriorityTask, and that function is the only code that resets the run state (lines 1094, 1098 and 1112). prvCheckForRunStateChange (line 836) loops `while( pxThisTCB->xTaskRunState == taskTASK_SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD )`, re-enabling interrupts each time to wait for a switch that never happens. It is called from vTaskEnterCritical (line 7089) and vTaskSuspendAll (line 3928). Nothing breaks the loop: a later prvYieldCore sends no new IPI because the run state is already SCHEDULED_TO_YIELD (line 360), and vTaskPreemptionEnable does not yield because taskTASK_IS_RUNNING is false for run state -2 (line 3143). The comments at lines 2306-2312 and 3214-3220 say the task must be evicted before the critical section is exited; that requirement is no longer met.

xTaskRemoveFromEventList, xTaskResumeFromISR and the two notify-from-ISR functions now report that no yield is needed whenever this core already had a yield pending, even if the newly readied higher-priority task can only run on this core. An ISR that relies on pxHigherPriorityTaskWoken therefore skips portYIELD_FROM_ISR, and that task waits until the next tick or critical-section exit. The new condition `if( ( xYieldPendingBefore == pdFALSE ) && ( xYieldPendings[ portGET_CORE_ID() ] != pdFALSE ) )` appears at lines 5504, 3531, 8218 and 8355. prvYieldForTask (line 932) skips every core where `xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ] != pdFALSE`, so the calling core is never reconsidered. Trigger: ISR A calls xQueueSendFromISR(q, &v, NULL) and readies a medium-priority task. Passing NULL is supported: the comment at line 5485 says the flag is set "in case the user is not using the xHigherPriorityTaskWoken parameter". This leaves xYieldPendings[0]=pdTRUE. ISR B then gives a semaphore that readies task H, while every other core runs a task at H's priority or higher. prvYieldForTask yields no core, the function returns pdFALSE, and H waits. The baseline returned pdTRUE here. task.h line 1324 documents the return value as "pdTRUE if resuming the task should result in a context switch".

The change alters SMP scheduling in four places (tick time-slicing, vTaskSwitchContext, and the return values of xTaskRemoveFromEventList, xTaskResumeFromISR and the two notify-from-ISR functions) but adds no test. Nothing exercises preemption-disable together with blocking, remote suspend/delete, or a yield that was already pending. diff.patch changes only tasks.c. The export has no test directory (a glob for test/tests folders returns nothing). The two high findings above, a self-block that does not block and a remote-suspend livelock, are exactly the cases a test of the new vTaskSwitchContext branch would hit.

After any yield request reaches a core running a preemption-disabled task, xYieldPendings stays pdTRUE. Every critical-section exit by that task then raises a yield trap that takes both global kernel locks and is refused, which adds overhead and lock contention on a hot path for all cores. The new branch writes `xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ] = pdTRUE;` each time it refuses a switch. vTaskExitCritical copies `xYieldCurrentTask = xYieldPendings[ xCoreID ]` and calls `portYIELD()` whenever it is set (lines 7211-7223). vTaskSwitchContext takes portGET_TASK_LOCK and portGET_ISR_LOCK (lines 5225-5226) before reaching the refusal, so every taskENTER/EXIT_CRITICAL pair in that task costs a full context-save trap until preemption is re-enabled.

The same snapshot-and-compare block is copied into four functions, with inconsistent comparisons, so any later fix to the 'did this call pend a yield' rule must be made four times. `BaseType_t xYieldPendingBefore = xYieldPendings[ portGET_CORE_ID() ]; prvYieldForTask( ... ); if( ( xYieldPendingBefore == pdFALSE ) && ...` is repeated at lines 3527-3532, 5500-5505, 8214-8219 and 8351-8356. Two copies test `!= pdFALSE` and two test `== pdTRUE`. A small helper wrapping prvYieldForTask that returns whether it newly pended a yield on the calling core would keep the four in step.

Any pipeline with an ENTROPY distributional metric produces a script that crashes when run, because `.otherwise()` is chained onto an aggregate column instead of a `when()` column. _distributional_agg_expr returns `F.sum(F.when({cv} > 0, -{p} * F.log({p}))).otherwise(F.lit(0.0))`. The `when(...)` call closes inside `F.sum(...)`, so `.otherwise` is called on the `F.sum` result. Spark's Column.otherwise throws "otherwise() can only be applied on a Column previously generated by when()" as soon as the expression is built, so the `_dist_i = _shares_i.groupBy(...).agg(...)` line fails. Trigger: `_pipeline_full()` in the tests configures `region` with ENTROPY. The tests only run `ast.parse`, so this passes them.

The MODE metric returns an arbitrary category per entity-period, not the dominant one, so every MODE column and the Layer 3 features built from it (ULT_MES, PREV_MES, REC) hold non-deterministic wrong values. MODE emits `F.first(F.col("{cat_col}"), ignorenulls=True)` inside `_shares_i.groupBy(ids, time).agg(...)`. `_shares_i` is itself a groupBy result with no ordering, so `first` takes whatever row the shuffle delivers first. It ignores `{cat_val_col}`, the per-category aggregate that defines the mode (the code would need something like `F.max_by(cat, cat_val)`). Trigger: `_pipeline_all_metrics()` configures MODE.

The output does not meet Plan 16. Instead of a lazy callable that takes a SparkSession, the generator emits a flat script that needs a pre-existing global `spark` and overwrites a table at every step as it runs. docs/general_plan.md:449 and :462 require a PySparkOutput 'containing a callable that, when invoked with a SparkSession, executes the full pipeline' and that 'All transformations are lazy until the returned callable is invoked'. `_HEADER` (lines 20-24) imports SparkSession but never builds or accepts one. Every build_* step ends with `.write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable(...)` (e.g. line 78), which is an eager action, and later steps read those tables back with `spark.read.table`. Despite this, the class docstring says 'All generated transformations are lazy'. Trigger: `FeatureStoreOutput.save()` writes script.py, and running it with `spark-submit script.py` fails at the first `spark.read.table` with NameError: name 'spark' is not defined. In a notebook it immediately overwrites five tables.

CREC ignores the feature's window size, so CREC features for different windows (e.g. `__CREC__BACKWARD__3` and `__CREC__BACKWARD__6`) are identical one-period growth rates. The CREC branch emits `((col - F.lag(col, 1).over(base_window)) / F.when(prev != 0, prev))` and never reads `w` or `frame_w`. TemporalFeature treats CREC as a windowed operator: window_size is required and appears in column_name. TemporalSpaceBuilder emits one CREC feature per entry in time_windows for every NUMERIC or TEMPORAL column. Trigger: `_pipeline_pivot_only()` with `time_windows=[3, 6]` generates both features with the same expression.

RATIO emits a plain windowed sum, identical to SUM_U, so every RATIO feature is a mislabelled duplicate rather than a ratio. `if op == TemporalOperator.RATIO: return f'F.sum({col_ref}).over({frame_w}).alias("{alias}")'` is the same expression as the SUM_U branch. No division and no second window appear. RATIO is only generated when `composed_windows` is set (TemporalSpaceBuilder._COMPOSED_OPERATORS), so any user who opts in gets wrong values.

Field names and categorical values are pasted into generated Python source without escaping. A quote in a value breaks the script or rewrites the filter, and a crafted value could inject code that runs when the script executes. `f'(F.col("{cat_field.name}") == "{cat_val}")'` and `', '.join(f'"{c}"' for c in id_cols)` interpolate raw strings. The same file uses `!r` for table names, so it does not escape consistently. `_check_name_part` only rejects `__`. For example, `allowed_values=['12" pipe']` produces a SyntaxError, and a value like `A"), eval("..."), ("` produces valid code that runs eval. PivotSpaceBuilder also accepts a `domain_resolver` that reads values from the data. FeatureStorePipeline does not pass it today, so the data-derived path is not currently reachable through the pipeline.

A dataset whose source_reference is a SQL string produces a script that fails at runtime, because the generator always treats it as a table name. AbstractDataset documents `source_reference` as a 'Fully-qualified table name or SQL string', but every step emits `spark.read.table({src!r})` (lines 72, 123, 165). `spark.read.table("SELECT ...")` raises a parse/table-not-found error. The generator has no `spark.sql(...)` path.

The acceptance tests check only Python syntax and substrings, so they pass the runtime-crashing ENTROPY expression, the wrong MODE, CREC and RATIO logic, and the missing callable. Every assertion is either `_is_valid_python` (an `ast.parse` check) or a substring check such as `"crossJoin" in code` or `".over(" in code`. `test_combined_code_contains_all_steps` asserts `"features" in code` (line 157), which the comment `# --- Layer 3: temporal features ---` already satisfies even if the final-join step were missing. No test builds the expressions against a real or mocked SparkSession (the plan allows a mocked session), and no test pins the expression emitted for any individual metric or operator.

Distinct operator pairs PROM_U/PROM_P, SUM_U/SUM_P and FREQ/XM produce byte-identical expressions, so at least one operator in each pair may not implement its intended semantics and the output table carries duplicate columns. PROM_U and PROM_P both return `F.avg(col).over(frame_w)`. SUM_U and SUM_P both return `F.sum(col).over(frame_w)`. FREQ and XM both return `F.sum(F.when(col.isNotNull(), 1).otherwise(0)).over(frame_w)`. MEDIA_ABS is emitted as a median (`percentile_approx(col, 0.5)`). Nothing in the repo defines these operators, so the generator encodes guesses that nobody signed off.

Unknown temporal operators fall through to an identity expression without any error, so an operator added later would produce wrong features without failing. _temporal_pyspark_expr ends with `return f'{col_ref}.alias("{alias}")'` for any unmatched operator. In contrast, `_distributional_agg_expr` raises `ValueError(f"Unsupported distributional metric: {metric}")`.

The new module carries dead and duplicated code that misleads readers. The registration check in checkin is never enforced because the async isRegistered call is not awaited, so staff can check in a participant who is not registered for the event. Line 106 reads `if (!this.eventService.isRegistered(user!, event))`. EventService.isRegistered is `async` (event_service.ts:5), so it returns a Promise, which is always truthy, and `!Promise` is always false. Trigger: a staff member scans the QR code of a participant who has no row in event_users for that event. The guard is skipped, isCheckedIn is false, and `this.eventService.checkin(user!, event)` (line 116) inserts an event_checkins row. The 'Participante não registado no evento' branch can never run. The isCheckedIn call two lines below does use `await`, which shows the omission here is a mistake.

When a participant profile has no linked user, checkin crashes with a TypeError (a 500) instead of returning a handled error, and the un-awaited isRegistered rejection may also surface as an unhandled promise rejection. `const user = await User.findBy("participantProfileId", profile?.id);` can return null. There is no null check before `user!` is passed to isRegistered (line 106, not awaited), isCheckedIn (line 111) and checkin (line 116). Each of those reads `user.id` (event_service.ts:9, 19, 35). The awaited isCheckedIn then throws `Cannot read properties of null`. The earlier un-awaited isRegistered promise rejects with no handler attached.

The controller awaits `isCheckedIn` (events_controller.ts:111) and then calls `checkin`, which does `event.related("checkedInUsers").attach({[user.id]: ...})` with no transaction or onConflict. The migration adds `table.unique(["event_id", "user_id"])`, so a second concurrent insert throws. The scanner the dialog uses is configured with `allowMultiple={true}` and `scanDelay={0}` (scanner.tsx:19-20), and each detection calls `handleCheckIN(slug)` → `post(...)`, so a code held in view sends repeated POSTs for the same slug.

A staff member who is registered for an event cannot open the check-in scanner on that event's page, because the QR trigger is rendered only inside the not-registered block. The `<QrCode onClick={() => setScannerModalOpen(true)} />` element sits inside `{!isRegistered && ( <div ...> ... )}` (lines 290-317). For a staff user with isRegistered=true, that block is replaced by the 'Inscrito' indicator (line 329), so nothing can set scannerModalOpen to true even though EventCheckInDialog is still mounted at line 386.

EventCheckInDialog returns early before calling its hooks, which breaks React's Rules of Hooks; this may cause hook-order errors or lost form state when isOpen toggles. `if (!isOpen) { return null; }` (lines 18-20) comes before `const tuyau = useTuyau();` and `const { post } = useForm({ eventID })` (lines 22-26). The parent keeps the component mounted and toggles `isOpen={scannerModalOpen}` (page.tsx:388), so the number of hooks called changes between renders of the same instance. The early return is also unnecessary, because `<Dialog open={isOpen}>` already controls visibility.

The check-in path contains dead or misleading code: a no-op event.save(), a try/catch that cannot catch request failures, a stray FIXME, and an optional chain after a null check. checkin() calls `await event.save();` without modifying the event. event_check_in_dialog.tsx:29-50 wraps Inertia `post(...)`, which reports failures through callbacks rather than throwing, in try/catch. events_controller.ts:97 has `// FIXME: change this to User when slug in user is ready`, and line 104 uses `profile?.id` right after `if (!profile) return`.

The check-in route puts a participant slug in the events resource's id position and takes the event id from an unvalidated body field, so a request without eventID produces a query error (500) instead of a 4xx. `router.post("/:slug/check-in", [EventsController, "checkin"])` sits in the `/events` group, where sibling routes use `/:id/...`. The handler reads `request.input("eventID")` with no validator and passes it straight to `Event.findOrFail(eventID)` (events_controller.ts:93-95).

Wrapping the shared CredentialScanner in a fixed `w-64` div also shrinks the scanner on the existing QR scanner page, which this feature did not ask for. `<div className="w-64">` now wraps `<Scanner .../>` in the shared component. inertia/pages/qrscanner/page.tsx:19 also renders CredentialScanner inside a `w-3/4` column, so that page's scanner is now capped at 16rem.

The scanner trigger is a bare SVG icon with an onClick handler, so keyboard and screen-reader users cannot reach or identify it. `<QrCode onClick={() => setScannerModalOpen(true)} />` renders a lucide SVG with no button wrapper, tabIndex, role or aria-label. The adjacent register action uses the `<Button>` component.

The new relations use `public x!:` instead of the `declare` form every other Lucid relation in these models uses, which is inconsistent and may emit a class field that shadows the ORM-managed property. event.ts:57 has `public checkedInUsers!: ManyToMany<typeof User>;` and user.ts:56 has `public checkedInEvents!: ManyToMany<typeof Event>;`. The neighbouring relations are written `declare registeredUsers: ManyToMany<typeof User>;` and `declare eventsRegistered: ManyToMany<typeof Event>;`.

The 'Resolve source workflow run ID' step declares the `env:` key twice, so GitHub's workflow parser will reject the file and the remediation workflow will never run on any trigger. Lines 29-31 and 32-34 are identical `env:` mappings (`GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`, `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}`) on the same step. YAML mapping keys must be unique, and GitHub Actions rejects such files with "'env' is already defined". Trigger: any completion of 'Weekly Grype Security Scan', or any manual dispatch, finds an invalid workflow file and no job starts.

The Resolve step's shell script cannot be parsed. It has two `else` branches and heredoc terminators that will never match, so the step fails on every trigger (including the normal workflow_run path), and no artifact is downloaded and no issue is created. The `if ... elif ... else` block opens a second `else` at line 94 before the closing `fi` at line 163, which is a bash syntax error. Separately, the block scalar's base indentation is 10 spaces (`set -euo pipefail`, line 36), so the `PY` terminators at lines 93 and 162 keep 2 leading spaces. A plain `<<'PY'` heredoc only ends on a line that is exactly `PY`, so the heredoc runs to EOF and `fi` is never seen. The Python body would also get leading spaces and raise IndentationError. Bash parses the whole `if` compound before running any branch, so even the `workflow_run` branch at line 40 never executes. The two Python blocks (lines 42-93 and 95-162) are near-duplicates, which suggests a half-finished edit that was never run.

The workflow_dispatch `run_id` input is pasted straight into the shell script, so whoever dispatches the workflow can run arbitrary commands with the job's `issues: write` token or inject extra `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` keys. Line 37 `[ -n "${{ inputs.run_id }}" ]` and line 38 `echo "id=${{ inputs.run_id }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` expand the expression before bash runs, so an input like `"; curl … ; echo "` becomes shell code. The value is never checked to be numeric and is later placed in an API URL path (`/actions/runs/{run_id}/artifacts`, line 183). Dispatch needs write access, which limits who can trigger it. The input should be passed through `env:` and checked against `^[0-9]+$`.

The fallback that looks up the latest successful weekly scan filters on `branch=pre-update-release`, but the weekly scan runs on a schedule, and scheduled runs are recorded against the default branch. The manual-dispatch-without-run_id path may therefore never find a run. `weekly-security-grype.yml` triggers on `schedule` (cron `0 12 * * 3`). It only checks out `pre-update-release` via `ref: ${{ env.BASE_BRANCH }}`, so its run's `head_branch` is the default branch. Lines 51 and 105 set `branch = "pre-update-release"`, and the runs query uses it (lines 75-79, 129-133). Unless someone has manually dispatched the scan from `pre-update-release`, the query returns no runs and the step exits with 'No successful runs found'.

When a weekly scan reports no fixable vulnerabilities, the existing open tracking issue is neither updated nor closed, so it keeps recommending upgrades that have already been made. Line 292 sets `has_recommendations = "false"` when `ordered` is empty, and the only issue step is gated by `if: steps.report.outputs.has_recommendations == 'true'` (line 319). No branch updates or closes the issue found by title, so the last non-empty report stays open indefinitely.

The guard is gated on `github.actor`, so it is skipped whenever a human pushes to, or closes and reopens, a Dependabot PR. A skipped job counts as passing for required checks, so a regressing dependency update can merge unscanned. `if: github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]'` checks who triggered this event, not who authored the PR. A maintainer pushing a fix-up commit to the Dependabot branch fires `pull_request: synchronize` with `github.actor` set to the maintainer, so the `grype-guard` job is skipped. Checking `github.event.pull_request.user.login == 'dependabot[bot]'` would keep the gate tied to Dependabot PRs.

The 'underfixed' check blames the PR for every vulnerable package whose version changed. A Dependabot base-image bump that lowers High/Critical counts is still blocked whenever any OS package in the new image keeps a fixable High/Critical. `changed_vulnerable_pkgs` (lines 179-184) includes any package whose vulnerable-version set differs between the base and PR images. `underfixed_updates` (186-189) keeps those with any fixed High/Critical in the PR scan, and line 205 raises SystemExit before the count-regression check. For a `docker` ecosystem PR (e.g. `python:3.14-alpine3.21` → a newer tag), most OS package versions change, so one remaining fixable High in an untouched OS package fails the guard even though `pr_counts['High'] < base_counts['High']`.

The regression gate only compares counts per severity, so a PR that fixes one High and adds a different, not-yet-fixable High passes as 'no regression'. `critical_regression`/`high_regression` (lines 202-203) compare only `pr_counts` against `base_counts`, which come from `counts()` (Counter by severity). The other check, `underfixed_updates`, only catches packages with `fix.state == 'fixed'` (lines 129-130 via `fixed_high_critical_recommendations`). A new High with state `not-fixed` or `wont-fix` that replaces a removed High therefore leaves both checks green. Comparing vulnerability IDs per package would catch the swap.

The gate's scanner is whatever Grype release is 'latest' at run time, pulled by a mutable tag and given the Docker socket. The gate's verdict can change between runs, and an unverified image gets root-equivalent control of the runner. Line 36 resolves the tag from an unauthenticated call to `api.github.com/repos/anchore/grype/releases/latest`, which can also hit rate limits and fail the gate. Line 42 runs `docker pull "anchore/grype:${{ steps.grype-release.outputs.tag }}"` with no digest. The scan steps mount `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` (line 68). Actions are pinned to major tags only (`actions/checkout@v6`, `actions/upload-artifact@v7`, and `actions/github-script@v8` in the remediation workflow). This copies the pre-existing weekly-scan pattern.

The artifact download sends the GITHUB_TOKEN bearer header to the archive URL, and Python's urllib keeps that header when following the redirect to the storage host. This may leak the token off api.github.com and may make the download fail. Lines 202-206 build `dl_req` for `selected["archive_download_url"]` with `"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"`, and line 209 `urllib.request.urlopen(dl_req, ...)` follows GitHub's 302 to a pre-signed blob URL. urllib's default redirect handler copies the request's non-content headers to the new request.

The tracking issue is found by title alone, so the bot will write its report into any open issue with that title, including one opened by an outside user, who can then edit the 'recommendations' that maintainers read. `issues.find(i => i.title.toLowerCase() === title.toLowerCase() && !i.pull_request)` has no filter on `i.user.login` (e.g. `github-actions[bot]`), and then calls `github.rest.issues.update` on that issue's number.

Prelink copies are never cleared, so a library that no longer needs rewriting is still replaced by an old rewritten copy left by an earlier build, and ILLink then trims and ships the old version of that library. The swap target picks any ResolvedFileToPublish .dll for which `Exists('$(IntermediateOutputPath)prelink/%(Filename)%(Extension)')` is true and points it at that file. It does not check whether the current run produced the file. PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner.RunTask only calls `Directory.CreateDirectory (OutputDirectory)` (PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner.cs:46) and writes a file only when `ProcessAssemblyDesigner` returns true. It never deletes anything. The `<FileWrites>` entry is added in the inner per-RID build, where IncrementalClean is deliberately removed (AssemblyResolution.targets:23-26), so nothing else cleans the directory. Trigger: build once with library X v1, which has a legacy Resource class; prelink/X.dll is written. Then upgrade X to v2, built with the designer assembly. The task reruns because its inputs are newer, but FixLegacyResourceDesignerStep.ProcessAssemblyDesigner returns false for v2 ("has already been processed" / "has no designer"), so nothing is written. Exists() still finds the v1 prelink copy, so ResolvedFileToPublish is pointed at the old v1 code before ILLink runs.

The rewrite target counts as up to date based on a single stamp file. If the prelink copies are deleted, or an assembly is added whose timestamp is older than the stamp, the target is skipped and legacy libraries go to ILLink without being rewritten, with no error at build time. `Inputs="@(_PreTrimmingAssembly)" Outputs="$(_AndroidStampDirectory)_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesigner.stamp"`. The prelink files are not listed as outputs. The update target only swaps files that `Exists()`, so when prelink/ is missing while the stamp is current, nothing is rewritten and nothing is swapped. In that case nothing fixes the library: this change removed the post-trimming FixLegacyResourceDesignerStep from PostTrimmingPipeline and removed the designer TrimmerRootDescriptor. The unrewritten library keeps reading its own Resource fields, which hold the IDs from its own compile. Elsewhere this repo tracks item-set changes with hash files (e.g. `_ResolvedUserAssembliesHashFile` in AssemblyResolution.targets); this target has no such check.

With NativeAOT and the trimmable typemap, `_AndroidRunNativeCompile` now depends on a target that does not exist in that configuration, so MSBuild stops with MSB4057. `DependsOnTargets="_PreTrimmingFixLegacyDesignerUpdateItems;NativeCompile"`. That target is defined only in Microsoft.Android.Sdk.TypeMap.LlvmIr.targets. Xamarin.Android.Common.targets:2880-2881 imports that file only when `'$(_AndroidTypeMapImplementation)' != 'trimmable'`. The trimmable path is a supported NativeAOT combination: TypeMap.Trimmable.targets:9 imports TypeMap.Trimmable.NativeAOT.targets, and `_ValidateTrimmableTypeMapRuntime` accepts NativeAOT. NativeAOT.targets is always imported for `_AndroidRuntime=NativeAOT` (Microsoft.Android.Sdk.targets:36), and a missing target in DependsOnTargets is a hard error. This path is experimental, which is why this is medium.

Every Verify run on the GCE path now fails at check 3 because the probe for non-wrapper binaries looks up a command name that includes literal double quotes. Even when `jq` is installed, the check reports it missing, and checks 4–11 (Trello, GWS auth, Alertmanager, sandbox image, DEPLOYED_REF, mongodb-mcp) never run. The probe is built with an unquoted heredoc: `nonwrapper_probe="$(cat <<SH ... binary_path="\$(command -v \"${binary}\" || true)"`. In an unquoted bash heredoc, a backslash escapes only `$`, backtick, `\` and newline, so `\"` stays as `\"`. The generated script therefore reads `binary_path="$(command -v \"jq\" || true)"`. `shell_single_quote` passes that through unchanged to `sudo docker exec <container> sh -c '...'`. Inside the `$(...)`, dash parses `\"jq\"` as the word `"jq"` (with quote characters), so `command -v` finds nothing, `|| true` leaves `binary_path` empty, and the probe exits with `missing_binary:jq`. `jq` is the first entry in scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json and uses `install.method: system` (not a wrapper), so the first loop iteration hits `|| fail "Failed to validate runtime binary jq in ..."`. The outer call at line 361 then fails. Check 3 runs whenever `GCE_INSTANCE_NAME` is set, which covers both staging and production.

The runtime binary check now uses the manifest from the CI runner's checkout instead of the one baked into the deployed image. Verify can therefore check binaries the image was never built with, or skip ones it was, whenever the checked-out commit and the image's build commit differ. Line 357 sets `runtime_binary_manifest_in_repo="${repo_root}/scripts/docker/runtime-binaries.json"`, and line 252 runs `jq ... "${runtime_binary_manifest_in_repo}"` on the runner. The manifest inside the image (`/usr/local/share/openclaw/runtime-binaries.json`, installed by Dockerfile:135 and Dockerfile.sandbox:23) only gets `test -f` (lines 240-243); its contents are never read. The removed probe ran `jq` on the in-image manifest, so the image was always checked against its own manifest. .github/workflows/verify.yml:35 uses `actions/checkout@v4` with no `ref`. deploy-staging-on-release.yml calls verify from a `workflow_run` trigger, where the default checkout is the default branch, but the image under test is built from `github.event.workflow_run.head_sha` on daisy/dev. If those branches differ, the two manifests may disagree.

The wrapper directory is now read from the CI runner's environment instead of the target image's environment, so Verify would look in the wrong place if an image ever set a different `OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN`. `runtime_wrapper_bin="${OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN:-/opt/daisy/bin}"` is evaluated on the runner, and verify.yml never sets that variable, so the value is always the default. The removed probe evaluated the same expression inside the container (quoted `<<'SH'` heredoc), where the image's own `ENV OPENCLAW_RUNTIME_WRAPPER_BIN` applied (Dockerfile:25, Dockerfile.sandbox:4). The two match today only because both Dockerfiles hard-code /opt/daisy/bin.

About 170 lines of new remote-command and probe-generation shell logic arrived with no tests. The image branch of `build_target_direct_exec_command` copies the smoke-command parsing and validation from `build_direct_exec_smoke_command` instead of reusing it, and the shared backslash guard checks for the wrong pattern. Lines 186-206 repeat lines 91-113 (the `case "${smoke_command}" in "${binary}"|"${binary} "*)` suffix split, the metacharacter blocklist and the `read -r -a` / `printf '%q'` argument loop). Only the command prefix differs, so a fix to one copy will not reach the other. In both copies, `*'\\'*` is single-quoted and so matches two consecutive backslashes, not one. The fallback that finds the Sent folder by name never runs on IMAP servers without SPECIAL-USE or XLIST, which are the servers that need it. The name match also accepts only "Sent", so common names such as "Sent Items" and "Sent Messages" are missed. The only `dev` extra is in setup.py `extras_require`, and hatchling ignores setup.py. Without the extra, only runtime dependencies are installed. tests/test_server.py:7 and tests/test_container_console.py:5 both `import pytest`, and README lines 898 and 1047 tell users to run `pytest`. The new README line 65 says "installs all Python dependencies automatically (`uv pip install -e ".[dev]"`)".

The workspace folder and interpreter path are hard-coded to `/workspaces/ProxmoxMCP-Plus`. If the repository is cloned or forked under any other folder name, the container opens a path that doesn't exist, postCreateCommand runs in the wrong place, and VS Code points at a missing interpreter. Line 7 sets `"workspaceFolder": "/workspaces/ProxmoxMCP-Plus"` and line 20 sets `"python.defaultInterpreterPath": "/workspaces/ProxmoxMCP-Plus/.venv/bin/python"`. No `workspaceMount` is set, so Dev Containers uses its default mount, `/workspaces/<local folder name>`. The two paths only match when the clone folder is named exactly `ProxmoxMCP-Plus`. Using `${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}` and `${containerWorkspaceFolder}` would avoid this.

`uv venv` runs inside the bind-mounted checkout. A contributor who already created `.venv` on the host, as the README's Installation section tells them to, may have it replaced by a Linux virtualenv that no longer works on the host. With uv versions that require `--clear` to replace an existing venv, the command may instead fail, and then nothing is installed in the container. postCreateCommand runs `uv venv` in the workspace folder, which is the host checkout mounted into the container, and creates `.venv` there. README line 99, in the existing Installation steps, runs `uv venv` in the same checkout on the host. .gitignore line 25 ignores `.venv`, so the host venv is present but untracked when the container is first created. uv is installed unpinned (Dockerfile line 17, `pip install --no-cache-dir uv`), so how it treats an existing `.venv` depends on which uv version the image build pulls.

'main'`, and fetch-skillset.ts:26 and download-from-github.ts:179 build URLs from that ref. Branch names containing `/` (e.g. `feature/x`) are also split wrongly, because `[^/]+` takes `feature` and moves `x` into the path. Cluster-mode URL resolution always picks the Keycloak Service's in-cluster DNS name. The documented `--keycloak/--namespace` invocation, run from an operator workstation, therefore sends the token request to a host that does not resolve, so "credentials are resolved automatically from the cluster" fails unless the user also passes `--server-url`. resolveURL returns `kc.Status.Endpoints.Admin` first. The operator always sets that field to `f"http://{name}-keycloak.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:8080"` (src/keycloak_operator/services/keycloak_reconciler.py:464-467), and `public` gets the same value, so the later fallbacks never run. The code's own comment says "the toolkit runs outside the cluster". Trigger: `keycloak-migrate import-users --keycloak my-keycloak --namespace keycloak-system --realm my-realm`, exactly as in docs/how-to/migration-toolkit.md and export-realms.md. ResolveFromCluster returns `http://my-keycloak-keycloak.keycloak-system.svc.cluster.local:8080`, then authenticate() calls http.DefaultClient.Do and gets a DNS lookup error. None of the docs or examples mention `--server-url` or port-forwarding for cluster mode.

decodeSecretKey base64-decodes a second time any secret value that happens to look like base64. Many real admin passwords and usernames get turned into random bytes, so authentication fails with 401 in cluster mode. client-go already returns `secret.Data` decoded. `if isBase64(decoded) { if b, err := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString(decoded); err == nil { return string(b), nil } }` then decodes again any value whose length is a multiple of 4 and which contains only [A-Za-z0-9+/=]. The operator generates passwords as 16 characters from `ascii_letters + digits + "!@#$%^&*"` (src/keycloak_operator/utils/kubernetes.py:1428-1429). About (62/70)^16 ≈ 14% of those are pure alphanumeric, and every such value is valid unpadded base64, so the password becomes 12 garbage bytes. A username like `root` or an existingSecret password like `Passw0rdPassw0rd` is mangled the same way. The "double-encoding" case it claims to guard against cannot work anyway: the operator decodes existingSecret values once and passes them to Keycloak unchanged (keycloak_reconciler.py:1315-1320).

The response parsing reads an `errors` count and `ERROR`/`FAILED` actions that Keycloak's Partial Import response may never contain, and it ignores `overwritten`. If so, the advertised "fail hard on errors > 0" check is dead code, and in `--mode overwrite` the summary reports overwritten users as neither added nor skipped. importResp declares only `Added`, `Skipped`, `Errors int `json:"errors"`` and `Results[].Action`. Line 217 collects details only when `r.Action == "ERROR" || r.Action == "FAILED"`. No `overwritten` field is decoded, and ImportResult/printImportSummary have no overwritten counter. Nothing in the repo documents a Partial Import response with an `errors` field. Real failures still surface as non-200 statuses, which importBatch handles separately. The `errors > 0` path that the ADR, the command help and the docs describe has no test and no evidence that the server ever triggers it.

When a batch fails at the HTTP level, or a token refresh fails, ImportUsers returns a nil result. The caller's "print partial result so user can see progress" then prints nothing, and the counts from batches that were already committed are lost. `return nil, fmt.Errorf("batch %d/%d failed: %w", ...)` (line 82) and `return nil, fmt.Errorf("token refresh failed ...")` (line 76) throw away the accumulated `result`. cmd/import_users.go:161-163 calls `printImportSummary(cmd, result)` on error, but that function returns early on `result == nil`. Only the `batchResult.Errors > 0` path (possibly dead, see above) returns the partial result. That leaves the common failure mode (a 409 in FAIL mode, or a 4xx/5xx) without the summary the docs tell the user to check ("Batches that completed before the failure are not rolled back").

The explicit-credentials mode accepts the master admin password only as a command-line flag, so it ends up in the process list and shell history. The docs' recommended `--password "$KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD"` still expands into argv. `f.StringVar(&importUsersOpts.password, "password", "", ...)` is the only way to supply the password in that mode. There is no env-var, file or stdin option. docs/how-to/migration-toolkit.md presents this as the CI-pipeline example (`--password "$KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD"`), and the expanded value is visible to `ps` and to CI step echoing. The secrets risk focus requires that secrets come from the environment.

Authentication is hard-wired to the master realm's `admin-cli` password grant. The tool can only run with full master-realm superadmin credentials, even though it writes to a single realm, so a least-privilege, realm-scoped account cannot be used. `tokenURL := fmt.Sprintf("%s/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token", ...)` with `client_id=admin-cli` and `grant_type=password`. There is no option to choose the auth realm or use a client_credentials service account. Cluster mode also requires RBAC to read Secrets in the Keycloak namespace. The infra risk focus is least privilege and blast radius.

Admin credentials can go over plain HTTP without any warning. The hostname fallback builds `http://` URLs, and an `http://` `--server-url` is accepted silently. `scheme := "http"` unless `kc.Spec.TLS.Enabled`. All HTTP calls use http.DefaultClient (no timeout) with context.Background(), so an unresponsive Keycloak hangs the command indefinitely with no way to cancel cleanly. `resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)` at lines 120 and 174. cmd/import_users.go:88 uses `ctx := context.Background()`, with no deadline and no signal handling.
